new.n: Gold coins lost through the ice, Blue Lake channel
new.pl: Channel narrows between Blue Lake and Baxter (old Bastion or Walker) Lake, just east of Baldwin Township
new.v: A pouch of gold coins; about $500 in gold coins spilled in a fish house
new.st: Blue Lake was once Bleau's Lake, after a French trapper whose cabin stood on the southwest corner. A man crossing thin ice at the channel narrows to Bastion (Walker) Lake broke through and dropped a pouch of gold coins in about 3 ft of water over mud and weeds. In the early 1920s commercial fishermen in a bunk fish house spilled about $500 in gold coins from their bib overalls, and most went through the ice. The north lake fits today's Baxter Lake, with Walker School (historical) beside it in GNIS.
new.t: Shallow-water hunt (3 ft, muck): waders and a waterproof detector at the channel narrows. Also check the trapper's cabin corner on the SW shore. Confirm the channel on a 1938 air photo. The water is public; ask for shore access.
src: Sherburne Co. Hist. Soc., "There's Gold in Them Thar Hills" (text via Neb, Oct 2026)

new.n: Jesse James box, five oaks north of the Judson bridge
new.pl: North bank of the Minnesota River across the Judson bridge, by the Swan Lake Outlet
new.v: A box of gold, coins and cash
new.st: Local legend says Jesse James buried a box of gold, coins and cash while dodging a posse, in a meadow inside a ring of five giant oaks next to a creek, between the river and the hillside just north of the Judson bridge. Rex McBeth and a Judson storyteller told it, and others have hunted for it. The house right of the bridge turned up Indian artifacts when its foundation was dug. The James-Younger gang did flee west across this country after the Northfield raid in September 1876, so the setting fits, but the cache rests on one oral source.
new.t: Look for the oldest open-grown oaks on the valley floor along the outlet creek; a 1938 air photo helps. There is an Indian site nearby: never dig artifacts or burials. Private land: permission first.

new.n: Camp Lincoln, 1862 Dakota prisoner camp (Sibley Park)
new.pl: Sibley Park, Mankato, at the mouth of the Blue Earth River
new.v: Site of the camp where about 300 condemned Dakota men were held
new.st: The condemned Dakota prisoners, about 300 men, were held at Camp Lincoln, at what is now Sibley Park, while President Lincoln reviewed their sentences; 38 were hanged in Mankato on 26 December 1862. A forum claim that a "Fort Lincoln" stood 5 miles south near the Red Jacket bridge is not supported; the marker there is Fort L'Huillier's. Land of Memories Park, on the west side of Sibley, is remembered as a Dakota camp.
new.t: LOOK ONLY. A city park and a place of Dakota grief, with Sibley Mound Cemetery next to it. No detecting.

new.pl: Pipe Lake, east of Cosmos (the exact site is withheld on the National Register record)
new.v: The only complete sod fort of the 1863 frontier forts in Minnesota
new.st: One of about 12 forts thrown up in spring 1863 after the Dakota War, and the only complete sod fortification of that period left in Minnesota. A landowner found it in his woods. A club dig turned up a bullet carved "1863" and a soldier's brass name plate, now at the Meeker County Historical Society. Listed on the National Register in 2003 (#03000576).
new.t: LOOK ONLY: private land, on the National Register, and already detected. See the finds at the Meeker County Historical Society in Litchfield.

set.pl: Blue Hill, the glacial mound in Blue Hill Township (GNIS 640287)
set.st: "Old Sherburne," a hermit in a skin-clothed dugout, was said to hold over $40,000 in gold coin from a business he sold back East. He died in 1882 and is buried in Blue Hill (Galbraith) Cemetery; his brother came from Indiana, searched a month and found nothing. The belief is that it lies in or near the Blue Hill glacial mound, about 75 ft high. A second legend says soldiers carrying the 1862 Fort Snelling to Fort Ripley payroll buried it in two saddlebags under oak roots when they heard of the uprising; McDonald's 1978 version puts it just north of Elk Lake along Battle Brook, on the Baldwin Township side, and says a fire burned the area and the spot was lost. No record of a lost army payroll has been found, and the 1862 Dakota annuity gold reached Fort Ridgely safely.
set.t: The pin is the Blue Hill mound. The payroll version has a second spot: Battle Brook north of Elk Lake (about 45.4869, -93.6267). The cemetery is look-only. Private land: permission first.
pinev: Pin moved about 10 km from a township guess to the GNIS Blue Hill summit (640287), the mound the story names

t-tr-le-sueur.st: The 1926 bronze plaque (DAR Anthony Wayne Chapter, 27 June 1926) reads "Near this spot stood Fort Le Hillier ... erected by Pierre Charles Le Sueur, who with twenty-seven men here spent the winter of 1700." It sits on gravel-pit land about 100 yd from the Blue Earth River, facing a hillside with a fenced treeline and homes; a local detectorist thinks the fort stood on the open meadow below. GNIS keeps a LeHillier locale at 44.1519, -94.0352.

t-tr-bremer-ransom.st: The U.S. Treasure Atlas vol. 5 version: half the money, $150,000 in $5 and $10 bills, in a canvas-wrapped metal box under a fence post along a 10-mile stretch of old State Hwy 52 between Chatfield and Rochester. (The Atlas wrongly has Bremer pushed from the car north of Rochester; he was released near Rochester.)
src: U.S. Treasure Atlas vol. 5 (Neb quote, Oct 2026)

t-tr-lake-city.st: The U.S. Treasure Atlas vol. 5 (nos. 656A-B) says Lake City holds several caches hidden by Prohibition bootleggers and by wealthy farmers and businessmen, and that a Rochester treasure hunter dug up three separate caches here. So caches here were real, and some are already gone.
